sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
We have measured Münster's garages since 2020, with a break from September 2025 to February 2026. Use has been fairly steady: in July and August the same garages have been 32–38% occupied in every year since 2020, while spring 2026 ran about 4 points below spring 2023 (34% against 38% in March and April).

Münster is steering cars off the street and into its garages, mainly through price and space. In 2022 the council gave up the parking on the Domplatz, whose west side has been public seating since October 2023 [4]. A 2024 parking concept for the centre and station area makes new residents' parking zones its core [6]; residents now pay €260 a year for a permit [5], far more than in most German cities in our set. From January 2026 the central street zone was extended to the station area, and the first hour there rose from €2.50 to €3.50, more than the €3.00 the city's garages now charge [12]. A March 2026 proposal to the district council would go further and largely remove street parking from Altstadt streets such as Königsstraße and Alter Steinweg, directing drivers to the garages; it had not been decided [15]. On Saturdays the 1,000-space Coesfelder Kreuz garage now works as park-and-ride on a two-year trial, with a €5 ticket that covers the bus into town for up to five people [8].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The garages are run by WBI, the city's own company, which has eight in the centre with about 3,900 spaces [16]. Its prices rose in 2022 [3] and again in January 2026 [12]. Our tariffs on file predate the 2026 increase. In April 2026 WBI announced it would convert its garages from paper tickets to number-plate recognition, starting with Bahnhofstraße [16]. A new guidance website shows free spaces in 19 car parks, updated every minute [9], and street parking has been payable through a choice of apps since 2020 [1].

Bicycle parking competes for the same space. A 2021 city proposal had WBI run a new station of over 2,000 bike spaces east of the main station, and floated converting the Bremer Platz garage into a bike garage as part of a mobility hub [2]. In our data that garage is the busiest in town. Public charging is being added mainly on the street, about 50 new stations in spring 2025 [10]. Demand for the centre is strong: bus ridership and subscriptions have grown with the Deutschlandticket [14], and a new counter recorded about 85,000 passers-by each on Prinzipalmarkt and Ludgeristraße over the first Advent weekend of 2025 [13].

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
With one main operator and the same €2.50 first-hour price almost everywhere in our data, price tells us nothing about which garages fill. Location does. The garages and car parks on the ring between the Altstadt and the station are the busiest, at 48% on weekdays and 63% at weekends: Bremer Platz (75%), Engelenschanze (62%) and the Schlossplatz car park, which doubles to 71% at weekends.

Inside the Altstadt the picture is mixed. Smaller garages such as Stubengasse and Münster-Arkaden run at 40–45%. The two largest, Aegidii and Theater, with about 750 spaces each, average only 26%. The garages by the harbour, more than a kilometre out, are quieter still (about 25%). Unusually for our cities, Münster's garages are slightly busier at weekends than on weekdays overall.
